documents.unit: BaylorITS and Office of the Provost
documents.title: Baylor's Generative AI Policy
documents.date_or_term: current; text from Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/)
documents.summary: Baylor ITS and the Provost set nine university-wide guidelines on generative AI. They welcome AI, require human review, data protection and honor-code handling of misuse, and tell course instructors to specify permitted use and student documentation. The page also lists licensed tools and guides.
documents.stance_why: The page says Baylor "embraces" AI but sets no per-course rule; instead "Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools", so the decision is handed to instructors, which is delegates.

units.why: The opening sentence states the institutional position: "Baylor embraces Generative Artificial Intelligence as an effective tool". That is a default welcoming stance, so P02, addressed to all, informs, encourage.
units.anchor: Baylor embraces Generative Artificial Intelligence as an effective tool

units.why: The sentence grounds AI use in Baylor's Christian identity: "human conscience and intelligence are endowed by our Creator and cannot be replicated or replaced by artificial intelligence". It is a principle setting the institutional framework (P56), not a rule on a use; it is closer to a principle than to P53 harms.
units.anchor: cannot be replicated or replaced by artificial intelligence

units.why: "Existing university policies will apply to the use of AI" sets the scope principle that AI use falls under existing rules, an institution-wide framework statement (P56) rather than the human-collaborator analogy of P45.
units.anchor: Existing university policies will apply to the use of AI to the greatest extent possible

units.why: "humans must retain the final decision-making authority" is a principle that AI does not make employment, financial or mission-critical decisions. P46 is only about grades, so I chose P56 as the framework principle; modality must.
units.anchor: humans must retain the final decision-making authority

units.why: New platforms "must undergo review and approval by BaylorITS and the Office of the Provost before adoption" requires vetting of AI tools, including those built by students. P50 (vetted tools) fits better than P65, which concerns contracts and data sharing.
units.anchor: must undergo review and approval by BaylorITS and the Office of the Provost before adoption

units.why: "Use of AI tools in academic programs should be transparent" asks for openness about AI use, a disclosure norm (P24), with should modality.
units.anchor: Use of AI tools in academic programs should be transparent

units.why: "Confidential data should be restricted for non-public AI tools" is a data-protection rule tied to data security standards, so P50.
units.anchor: Confidential data should be restricted for non-public AI tools

units.why: "Actions resulting from AI tool usage are the sole responsibility of the user" makes users accountable for outputs and legal compliance, so P29, must, addressed to all users.
units.anchor: Actions resulting from AI tool usage are the sole responsibility of the user

units.why: "Misuse of AI by students should be reported to the Honor Council" routes student misuse into the honor-code process, i.e. misconduct handling (P36); addressed to instructors who report.
units.anchor: Misuse of AI by students should be reported to the Honor Council

units.why: "AI policy violations will be addressed by the appropriate academic dean's office and the Office of the Provost" assigns who handles violations; it is the enforcement process, P36, directed at the institution (admin).
units.anchor: AI policy violations will be addressed by the appropriate academic dean’s office

units.why: "Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools" leaves the rule to each instructor, so P04 (not P09, since no syllabus is named).
units.anchor: Course instructors should specify the permitted use of AI tools

units.why: The same sentence asks instructors to specify "the responsibilities of students to document what and how tools and data were used", a documentation/disclosure expectation (P24; P26 needs full logs which are not stated).
units.anchor: responsibilities of students to document what and how tools and data were used

units.why: "All AI-generated results must undergo human review to ensure accuracy before being used" is a verification duty on AI output, P31.
units.anchor: All AI-generated results must undergo human review to ensure accuracy before being used

units.why: The text says AI "can summarize research content, analyze data, ... or even operate as a research assistant", describing research uses as potential; it governs AI in research (P62) and is descriptive, so informs.
units.anchor: Generative Artificial Intelligence has the potential to accelerate research

units.why: "the research community must remain nimble and adjust to AI utilization methods quickly" acknowledges that practice will change as the technology does, so P54.
units.anchor: the research community must remain nimble and adjust to AI utilization methods quickly

units.why: "the educational opportunities and resources will be updated periodically" states the site content will be revised; provisional/updated guidance, P54.
units.anchor: the educational opportunities and resources will be updated periodically

units.why: The Instructor Guide is offered "to help instructors navigate the use of generative AI", an institutional support for instructors learning about AI, so P63.
units.anchor: This guide is to help instructors navigate the use of generative AI

units.why: "This guide is to help students navigate the use of generative AI" is student-facing guidance; no type covers student guidance resources (P63 is faculty-only, P44 teaches professional skill), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: This guide is to help students navigate the use of generative AI
units.uncovered_note: The university provides a student guide to navigating generative AI.

units.why: The "Generative AI Literacy Course" is "A Canvas-based course to get you up to speed on GenAI", an institutional course teaching AI literacy; it is not about professional skills expressly, so UNCOVERED rather than P44.
units.anchor: A Canvas-based course to get you up to speed on GenAI
units.uncovered_note: The university offers a Canvas-based AI literacy course for the community.

units.why: "Recommended Syllabus Statements" are offered for instructors (access behind Box); a provided template resource for communicating AI rules, which no type covers (P09 requires a statement; this only recommends templates).
units.anchor: Recommended Syllabus Statements
units.uncovered_note: The university provides recommended syllabus statements on AI for instructors.

units.why: Under "Select Baylor-Licensed GenAI Platforms" the page lists Microsoft Copilot Chat among others as university-licensed tools, which is a sanctioned tool provision (P17).
units.anchor: Microsoft Copilot Chat is a GenAI tool used to query complex questions

documents.title: Suggestions for Dealing with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Produced Assignments
documents.date_or_term: current; text from Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/)
documents.summary: The Office of Academic Integrity gives faculty strategies for AI-produced essays: communicate expectations, redesign assignments, use in-class writing and oral checks, and look for tell-tale errors. It also records that Turnitin AI detection was dropped after 2023.
documents.stance_why: The page is faculty advice; it only states that "submitting work produced by an AI system as their own is not acceptable" and leaves whether and how AI may be used to each instructor, so it sets no use rule itself: delegates.

units.why: The Provost update says the University will "allow the AI detection feature within Turnitin.com to expire" because of accuracy uncertainty. It is a decision not to rely on a detector, P39.
units.anchor: allow the AI detection feature within Turnitin.com to expire at the end of December 2023

units.why: "Utilize the University's recommended syllabus statements" asks instructors to put a syllabus statement in place, P09 (should-level suggestion).
units.anchor: Utilize the University's recommended syllabus statements for undergraduate student classes

units.why: "Discuss this issue with students on the first day of class, communicate your expectations" tells instructors to talk through AI rules at course start; P09 is syllabus-specific, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Discuss this issue with students on the first day of class
units.uncovered_note: Instructors discuss AI expectations orally with students on the first day of class.

units.why: "submitting work produced by an AI system as their own is not acceptable and is a violation of Baylor's Honor Code" is a ban on passing off AI work. I chose P19 (the ban) over P36 because the core content is what students may not do; the honor-code label is secondary.
units.anchor: submitting work produced by an AI system as their own is not acceptable

units.why: "Familiarize yourself with AI systems" and try past prompts so assignments can be designed; this advises instructors to learn AI before designing, P63.
units.anchor: Familiarize yourself with AI systems

units.why: "Require writing to be done in class (by hand if possible)" moves assessment into supervised unassisted writing, P33.
units.anchor: Require writing to be done in class (by hand if possible)

units.why: "Write essay prompts that are specific enough" so vague AI essays are not possible is an assignment redesign against AI, P35.
units.anchor: Write essay prompts that are specific enough to other class assignments

units.why: "Consider incorporating personal reflections from students into essays" redesigns assignments to resist AI, P35.
units.anchor: Consider incorporating personal reflections from students into essays where possible

units.why: Advising "incorporating something about very recent events into essays" because AI "appear not to be very good" after 2021 is an assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: consider incorporating something about very recent events into essays

units.why: "Require both in your essays, where possible, and then look for errors" uses citations and reference lists as an AI-resistant assignment feature, P35.
units.anchor: Require both in your essays, where possible, and then look for errors

units.why: "submit multiple drafts of an essay (using ... a scaffolding approach" restructures assignments around process, P35.
units.anchor: requiring students to submit multiple drafts of an essay

units.why: "so that a student's outside-of-class writing can be compared to his/her writing that is produced in class" uses in-class writing as process evidence to spot misuse, P40.
units.anchor: outside-of-class writing can be compared to his/her writing that is produced in class

units.why: "Incorporate a verbal exam requirement tied to an essay so that students ... discuss what they are turning in" checks understanding orally, P34.
units.anchor: Incorporate a verbal exam requirement tied to an essay

units.why: "Look for vague general comparisons" is a manual cue for identifying suspected AI essays, process evidence for detection, P40.
units.anchor: Look for vague general comparisons

units.why: "Look for factual claims that are asserted confidently but turn out to be false" is a content cue for spotting AI work, P40.
units.anchor: Look for factual claims that are asserted confidently but turn out to be false

units.why: "Look for claims that are backed up with citations of evidence but evidence that doesn't support the claims" is another manual cue for identifying AI work, P40.
units.anchor: Look for claims that are backed up with citations

documents.title: Is using ChatGPT for coursework considered cheating?
documents.summary: A library FAQ says whether ChatGPT may be used depends on each instructor, advises asking before starting, and notes that presenting a fully ChatGPT-written paper as your own breaches integrity principles.
documents.stance_why: The answer begins "It depends. ... it’s up to each instructor to create policies", handing the decision to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: "it's up to each instructor to create policies for classroom use" places the decision with instructors, P04.
units.anchor: it’s up to each instructor to create policies for classroom use

units.why: "if your instructor doesn't allow it, it would be cheating" classifies disallowed AI use as cheating, P36.
units.anchor: if your instructor doesn’t allow it, it would be cheating

units.why: "Always ask your instructor what their policies are" tells uncertain students to ask first, P10.
units.anchor: Always ask your instructor what their policies are

units.why: "it's still against the principles of academic integrity to represent a paper entirely written by ChatGPT as your own" bars passing off AI-written work even when AI is allowed, P19.
units.anchor: against the principles of academic integrity to represent a paper entirely written by ChatGPT

notes: Text for the ITS page and Honor Code page come from Wayback captures. Honor Code page is faculty-facing essay advice. Coder B: UNCOVERED units are student-facing resources, oral first-day discussion, and recommended syllabus statements.
